questions.prompt: Is this program well-formed, and if so what does it return?
options: Well-formed; returns 2, because `T` is deduced as `double`
Well-formed; returns 1, because `T` is deduced from the first argument as `int`
Ill-formed: `T` is deduced as `int` from one argument and as `double` from the other
Ill-formed: the call is ambiguous between `biggest<int>` and `biggest<double>`
questions.explanation: Each parameter/argument pair is deduced independently: the first gives `T = int`, the second `T = double`, and conflicting deductions make deduction fail, so there is no viable function. Deduction never considers the usual arithmetic conversions, so the "common type" answer is the tempting wrong one. `biggest<double>(1, 2.5)` would compile, because explicitly specified parameters no longer take part in deduction and `1` then converts.

The expression `r` has type `const int`; references are stripped from an expression's type before anything else happens. Because `P` is the non-reference `T`, top-level cv-qualifiers of `A` are dropped as well, so `T = int` and the parameter is a fresh copy. `const int&` is tempting if you think of deduction as copying the declared type of the variable, which it does not.

questions.prompt: What is `T` deduced as in the call `g(i)`?
options: Nothing: an lvalue cannot bind to `T&&`, so the call is ill-formed
questions.explanation: `T&&` where `T` is a function template parameter is a forwarding reference. For an lvalue argument, deduction uses "lvalue reference to `A`" in place of `A`, giving `T = int&`, and reference collapsing turns `int& &&` into `int&`. With `T = int` the parameter would be `int&&`, which cannot bind an lvalue; that rule is what the last option misremembers.

questions.prompt: Which of the two calls in `demo` is well-formed?
options: Both: `2` converts to `double` in each case
questions.explanation: In `scale_a`, the second parameter deduces `T = int`, which conflicts with `T = double` from the vector, so deduction fails and #1 is ill-formed. In `scale_b`, `std::type_identity_t<T>` is the nested name `std::type_identity<T>::type`, a non-deduced context, so `T = double` comes only from the vector and `2` is then converted like an ordinary argument. Conversions are never considered during deduction, which is why the first option is wrong.

options: Yes: `T` is deduced as `std::initializer_list<int>`, just as for `il`
No: a braced list makes the parameter a non-deduced context, so `T` cannot be deduced
Yes: `T` is deduced as `int`, from the first element
questions.explanation:
A braced-init-list has no type. Unless the parameter is `std::initializer_list

` or a reference to an array, an initializer-list argument makes the parameter a non-deduced context, and `T` is left undeduced, so the call is ill-formed. The tempting answer comes from `auto`: `auto il = {1, 2, 3};` deduces `std::initializer_list` by a special rule for `auto`, and `f(il)` then deduces from an ordinary expression.

A default template argument is used only when the parameter is neither specified nor deduced. In `kind(1)`, `T` is deduced as `int` from the argument, so the default is ignored. In `kind()`, the only function parameter relies on its default argument, which is a non-deduced context, so `T` falls back to `double` and `{}` value-initializes it. Without the default template argument, `kind()` would be the compile error of the third option.

questions.prompt: In which of these function parameter types is `T` in a non-deduced context, so that a call `f(x)` can never deduce `T`?
questions.explanation: The nested-name-specifier of a qualified type name is a non-deduced context: the compiler would have to invert an arbitrary metafunction, which it cannot. This is why `std::forward<T>` takes `typename std::remove_reference<T>::type&` and must be called with an explicit `T`. The other forms are all built from `T` with compound type constructors (references, pointers, template-ids, function types and arrays), and all of them can be deduced from a matching argument type.

questions.prompt: Which of the calls in `demo` are well-formed?
questions.explanation: [temp.deduct.call] lists the only differences allowed between the adjusted parameter and argument types; one is that when `P` is a class template specialization or a pointer to one, `A` may be a derived class, so #1 deduces `T = int` from the base `Base<int>`. User-defined conversions are not on the list: `Wrapper<T>` cannot match `int`, and the converting constructor is invisible to deduction, so #2 is ill-formed. A non-template `void wrap(Wrapper<int>)` would accept `1`, which is why #2 looks plausible.
